Multiplies length and width but omits height.
Doubles the correct product after multiplying all dimensions.

questions.question_text: A room measures $5$ m by $4$ m by $3$ m. What is its volume?

options.why: Adds the dimensions instead of multiplying.
Finds floor area and omits height.
Multiplies the correct volume by two.

questions.question_text:
A cube has edge length $4$ cm.
What is its volume?

options.why: Adds the three equal edge lengths.
Squares the edge instead of cubing it.
Multiplies the edge by itself and then by $3$.

questions.question_text: Which unit belongs on the volume $9\times2\times5=90$ when dimensions are in centimetres?

options.why: Uses an area unit after multiplying three dimensions.
Uses a length unit for a three-dimensional measure.
Changes centimetres to metres without converting the dimensions.

questions.solution_text: Three centimetre dimensions produce cubic centimetres.

questions.question_text:
A prism has volume $180\text{ cm}^3$, length $10$ cm and width $3$ cm.
What is its height?

options.why: Divides the volume by the width only.
Subtracts both known dimensions from the volume: $180-10-3=167$.
Multiplies the known dimensions but does not divide the volume.

questions.question_text:
A box measures $8$ cm by $5$ cm by $2$ cm.
A student calculates $8\times5\times2=80$.
Which final answer is correctly recorded?

options.why: Records area units after using three dimensions.
Records length units for a volume.
Changes the supplied centimetre dimensions to metre units.

questions.solution_text: The product of three centimetre dimensions is $80\text{ cm}^3$.

questions.question_text:
Which of the following calculations would give the volume of this cuboid?
The cuboid has dimensions 60 mm, 5 cm and 4 cm.

options.why: Adding the dimensions does not calculate the volume of a cuboid.
Although 60 mm equals 6 cm, adding dimensions still does not find volume.
The dimensions use mixed units, so this calculation is not consistent.

questions.solution_text: Convert 60 mm to centimetres: $60\text{ mm}=6\text{ cm}$. Volume is length times width times height, so the correct calculation is $6\times5\times4$.
